theme: Hear a just cause, O LORD, David’s appeal to integrity
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 17. This is a prayer of David, a man who is under attack and is asking God for vindication. Read it with Job in mind, and notice both the confidence of its opening and the hope of its closing line.
settingTheScene: Psalm 17 is attributed to David, and its tone is similar to some of Job’s. Both men appeal to God as a judge, both claim to have been faithful, and both are surrounded by enemies. David’s confidence in his integrity may sound proud at first reading. But look at what he is doing: he is not claiming perfection. He is claiming to be on the right side in a particular dispute, and he is bringing the case to God, the only judge who can settle it. The psalm ends with one of the loveliest hopes in the Psalter.
observation: The psalm begins, “Hear a just cause, O LORD; attend to my cry! Give ear to my prayer from lips free of deceit!” (v. 1).
“From your presence let my vindication come! Let your eyes behold the right!” (v. 2).
“You have tried my heart, you have visited me by night, you have tested me, and you will find nothing; I have purposed that my mouth will not transgress” (v. 3).
“Wondrously show your steadfast love, O Savior of those who seek refuge from their adversaries” (v. 7).
“Keep me as the apple of your eye; hide me in the shadow of your wings” (v. 8).
The enemies surround him. They are like a lion eager to tear (vv. 9-12).
“Arise, O LORD! Confront him, subdue him!” (v. 13).
The wicked have their reward in this life, with plenty of children and wealth (v. 14).
“As for me, I shall behold your face in righteousness; when I awake, I shall be satisfied with beholding your likeness” (v. 15).
interpretation:
The psalm begins with the language of a courtroom. David is making a case. “Hear a just cause.” He is not demanding mercy because he is weak. He is claiming that his cause is right. And he does so by saying that God has already examined him and found nothing wrong. “You have tried my heart…and you will find nothing.” This is not a statement that David is sinless. It is a statement that he has not done what his enemies accuse him of. It is also a statement that God is the final judge, and that David is willing to have his heart examined by him.

Job made the same appeal. “Oh, that I had one to hear me! Let the Almighty answer me!” The difference is that David is more confident that God will respond. He also adds a second image, one of intimacy and protection. “Keep me as the apple of your eye; hide me in the shadow of your wings.” The apple of the eye is the pupil, the most sensitive and protected part of the body. The shadow of the wings is a picture of a mother bird covering her young. David asks for two things at once: to be vindicated like a defendant in court, and to be held like a child. The psalm is a mixture of legal and tender language, and so is the gospel.

Verse 14 is worth noticing. The wicked are filled with the things of this life: wealth, children, a full belly. David does not envy them. He simply notes that this is all they have. Their “portion is in this life.” It echoes Psalm 73 and the end of Job.

And then the ending, which is the heart of the psalm. “As for me, I shall behold your face in righteousness.” David does not say that he wants to be wealthy or safe. He wants to see God’s face. He says that when he wakes, probably a reference to waking from death or from the long night of trouble, he will be “satisfied with beholding your likeness.” This is the same longing Job had in 19:26. “In my flesh I shall see God.” It is the hope that the Old Testament believers held onto: to see God.
connection: Jesus speaks of the pure in heart who “shall see God” (Matthew 5:8). Paul says, “Now we see in a mirror dimly, but then face to face” (1 Corinthians 13:12). John writes, “We know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2). Revelation 22:4 says, “They will see his face.” Jesus compared himself to a hen who gathers her chicks under her wings (Matthew 23:37).
application:
Ask God to examine your heart, as David does. Say “You have tried my heart” and then listen. Confess whatever comes to mind, and receive the forgiveness that is yours in Christ.

Ask yourself if you want to see God’s face more than anything else. If not, ask him to put that desire in you.

Take comfort in the picture of the apple of his eye. Say aloud, “I am the apple of his eye.” If that is hard to believe, bring that to him too.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to search your heart and show you what is wrong.
Ask him to hide you in the shadow of his wings.
Tell him you long to be satisfied in him.
